title: Why is the sky blue?
one_liner: Air scatters blue sunlight much more than red, so blue reaches your eyes from every part of the sky.

eli5.analogy: Sunlight is like a bag of coloured marbles, and the sky bounces the blue ones around the most.
eli5.body: Sunlight looks white but is really all the colours mixed. Tiny bits of air bump the blue light all over the sky [1]. So when you look up, blue comes at you from everywhere.

eli10.analogy: Like small waves bouncing off pebbles while big waves roll past.
eli10.body: Each colour of light has a different wavelength. Blue has short waves, red has long ones. Air molecules scatter short waves far more, so the sky fills with scattered blue [1][2].

eli15.analogy: A sieve that catches small grains and lets big ones through, but for light.
eli15.body: This is Rayleigh scattering: molecules much smaller than the wavelength scatter light with strength proportional to 1/wavelength^4 [2]. Blue near 450 nm scatters about 4 times more than red near 700 nm. Violet scatters even more, but sunlight has less of it and our eyes are less sensitive to it [3].

expert.analogy: The sky is a diffuse, wavelength-weighted re-radiator of the solar beam.
expert.body: The Rayleigh cross-section scales as lambda^-4 for size parameter x much less than 1 [2]. Integrated over the solar spectrum, the atmosphere's optical depth and the CIE photopic response, diffuse skylight peaks perceptually in the blue, while the direct beam reddens at low solar elevation [3][9].

diagram.caption: White sunlight enters the air, blue is scattered across the sky, and reaches your eye from all directions.
